content:
We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts: 135.80, 117.40, 70.50, 54.00, 43.70 ppm. Need to determine number of CH3 groups in the compound. Use carbon shifts to infer functional groups. Typically methyl carbon appears around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but here we have 43.70, 54.00, 70.50, 117.40, 135.80. 43.70 could be a methyl attached to heteroatom (e.g., O-CH3 ~55 ppm). 54.00 also O-CH3 or N-CH3. 70.50 could be carbon attached to O (like CH2O). 117.40 and 135.80 are aromatic/sp2 carbons. So maybe the molecule is anisole? Anisole (methoxybenzene) has aromatic carbons ~ 113-158, O-CH3 ~55 ppm. That's one methyl. But we have two peaks around 43.70 and 54.00, maybe two methyls attached to heteroatoms. Could be dimethoxybenzene (1,4-dimethoxybenzene) which has two O-CH3 groups (each ~55 ppm) and aromatic carbons. That would give two methyl groups. However we have also a 70.50 which could be a carbon attached to O (like O-CH2). But dimethoxybenzene doesn't have CH2. Could be a phenoxyethanol? Let's think.

We have 5 distinct carbon signals, meaning 5 unique carbon environments. If there are two methyl groups (both O-CH3) they'd be equivalent maybe if symmetric, giving one signal. But we have two separate signals at 43.70 and 54.00, maybe two different methyls (one attached to N, one to O). Could be something like anisidine? Not sure.

We could also get proton NMR to see methyl signals. Let's request proton NMR.
